title: Patterns in the Night Sky
seo_title: Grade 5 Night Sky Worksheets: Constellations, Seasons, Polaris and Earth's Orbit
standard_text: Represent data in graphical displays to reveal patterns of daily changes in length and direction of shadows, day and night, and the seasonal appearance of some stars in the night sky.
meta_desc: Free Grade 5 science worksheets on patterns in the night sky (NGSS 5-ESS1-2): stars rising and setting, Polaris and the Big Dipper, and seasonal constellations caused by Earth's orbit. 100 practice questions with answers.
key_big: Earth's spin moves the stars each night; its orbit changes them each season.
key_sub: Stars rise in the east and set in the west about 15° an hour. Different constellations are seen in different seasons because Earth orbits the sun.
body_html:
How to think about it

In one night: Earth spins once every 24 hours (about 15° each hour), so the stars seem to rise in the east and set in the west. Polaris, the North Star, stays almost still, and the Big Dipper circles around it.

In one year: Earth orbits the sun once every 365 days. At night we look away from the sun, out into a different part of space each season. So some constellations are seen only part of the year: Orion on winter evenings, Scorpius in summer.

Example

A star moves about 15° each hour. How far does it move in 4 hours?

15° × 4

Answer: 60°

Example

Why can't we see Orion on a summer night?

In summer, Orion is in the same direction as the sun.

It is up during the day, hidden by sunlight.

Answer: It is in the daytime sky.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the stars themselves move across the sky each night. Earth spins.
  • Thinking we see the same stars all year. The night sky changes with the seasons.
  • Mixing up the two motions: spinning (one day) and orbiting (one year).

faq.q: Why do stars move across the sky at night?
faq.a: They do not really move. Earth spins, so stars seem to rise in the east and set in the west, like the sun.

faq.q: Why do we see different stars in different seasons?
faq.a: Earth orbits the sun once a year. At night we face away from the sun, toward a different part of space each season.

faq.q: Why does Polaris stay in the same place?
faq.a: Polaris is almost straight above Earth's North Pole, along Earth's axis, so it barely moves as Earth spins.
From the United States, Orion is easiest to see on winter evenings. In summer it is in the daytime sky.

c: a group of stars that forms a pattern in the sky
items.e: Orion, Leo and the Big Dipper's group (the Great Bear) are patterns of stars.

It is close to Polaris, so it circles the pole and never sets.
It is closer than the moon.
items.e: Stars near Polaris stay above the horizon all night, all year.

items.q: Why do stars seem to move across the sky during the night?
c: The stars are flying across space.
items.e: As Earth spins toward the east, stars appear to rise in the east and set in the west, just like the sun.

items.q: Why do we see different constellations in winter and summer?
c: Earth moves around the sun, so at night we face different parts of space.
Clouds hide half the stars each season.
items.e: In one year Earth travels all the way around the sun, so the night sky changes with the seasons.

items.e: As Earth orbits, the evening sky changes month by month and repeats every year.
